items.title: Civic host led engagement
items.summary: Draft for BLOOM to edit: a locally rooted civic host brings neighbors together across difference and holds the question; BLOOM brings funding, methods, tools, and a peer network. Every build names its host.
items.body:
BLOOM partners with locally rooted organizations, called Civic Hosts, "that can bring neighbors together across difference to work through hard choices on AI and turn them into proposals decision makers can't ignore" (bloom-project.org). Local partners run the process; BLOOM brings the funding, methods, tools (CivicOS), coaching, and a peer network. In Utah the host was a coalition (Utah Common Ground, with Mormon Women for Ethical Government and others); in Central Oregon it is the Central Oregon Civic Action Project with local partners.

BLOOM's founding Civic Host cohort runs assemblies in 2027 (RFP out October 2026). What a host builds and learns in this studio feeds that cohort, and what the cohort learns flows back here.

Working in this frame:

- Every build names its civic host and the question the host is holding before the first screen is designed.
- The host is a person and an organization, not a platform. Put a name, a role, and a way to reach them on every public page.
- Design for the host's capacity: a small team, partners, volunteers, a few months. Not a full-time data team.
- "Across difference" is the point. Ask who in the place is unlikely to show up (by politics, age, geography, income, language) and make reaching them part of the build.

items.title: Listen widely, then deliberate representatively
items.summary: Draft for BLOOM to edit: open participation (an Open Poll and community conversations) maps where people stand; a representative assembly chosen by civic lottery then works through the tradeoffs and writes the recommendations.
items.body:
BLOOM's processes move through layers, each feeding the next. In Rahmin's words: "Open Poll is good at mapping the initial opinion landscape. We'll want more deliberative engagements to grapple with tradeoffs, find supermajority synthesis across them."

1. **Open participation.** Anyone can take part. An Open Poll puts short statements in front of people (agree, disagree, pass; add your own) and surfaces opinion groups. Community conversations, hosted by local partners in person and online, dig into the themes. Central Oregon: 400+ residents, six listening sessions, three opinion groups, strong common ground on transparency and community involvement.
2. **Representative deliberation.** A civic assembly selected by civic lottery ("a random, representative draw, much like a jury") to reflect the place's mix of age, geography, income, and political views. Delegates hear evidence, consider competing perspectives, work through tradeoffs, and write proposals together. Utah: 600+ Utahns in conversations, then 38 delegates over two days. Delegates are supported to take part (Central Oregon offers a stipend).
3. **Recommendations.** Proposals with their level of support, carried to the people who decide.

Working in this frame:

- Say which layer a build serves and design the hand-off: poll results and conversation themes become the assembly's briefing; the assembly's proposals become the report.
- The open layers welcome everyone. The assembly is representative by design: build lottery recruitment and support (stipends, childcare, transport, language) as carefully as the sessions themselves.
- Keep results honest: say who was heard and who was not, and lock reports until enough people have taken part.

items.title: Work through real differences
items.summary: Draft for BLOOM to edit: the goal is not agreement on everything. Bring different perspectives into the room, give people information and time, and find where there is enough common ground to act.
items.body:
From BLOOM's "How we work": "We don't ask people to agree on everything. We bring different experiences and perspectives into the room, give people the information and time to wrestle with real trade-offs, and find where there is enough common ground to act."

Utah showed what that can look like: 10 recommendations, each backed by at least 82% of a group chosen to reflect Utah's political makeup, and 92% support for the full package. A delegate: "I have a better outlook on my fellow citizens."

Rahmin's design lens for a people-powered process: start with story (of me, of us, of now), surface shared values and priorities before getting into policy, then let table-level conversations aggregate upward into a shared declaration.

Working in this frame:

- Show results by opinion group, not just overall. Common ground means every group agrees; make that visible (percent who agree, by group).
- Aim for supermajority agreement across groups, not a majority that outvotes a minority. Report the support level for every recommendation, including the ones that fell short.
- Give people the considerations behind a choice (evidence, competing views, tradeoffs) before asking them to decide.
- Never manufacture consensus: no made-up groups, no synthetic voices, no smoothing away the disagreement that remains.

items.title: AI in the loop, people hold the judgment
items.summary: Draft for BLOOM to edit: technology helps more people take part and helps everyone see what was said, without replacing human deliberation. AI synthesizes; it is never the authority, and its work is traceable.
items.body:
From BLOOM's "How we work": "We use technology to help more people participate, make sense of what we're hearing, and connect work across communities without replacing human deliberation. We build openly, show our work, and keep learning as we go."

Rahmin's Carnegie piece ("How AI Can Unlock Public Wisdom", 2025) sets the bar: AI should strengthen human judgment, not replace it; "AI analysis must be auditable and explainable"; and the main risk is participation-washing, input that looks impressive but changes nothing.

Working in this frame:

- Use AI to transcribe, theme, translate, and summarize. People facilitate, deliberate, and decide. Say plainly in the build where AI is used and where a person checks it.
- Every theme or summary traces back to the statements and quotes it came from, and a participant can say "that's not what we meant."
- Never let AI generate participant positions, votes, or quotes. Sample data is labeled sample.
- Prefer open-source, public-interest infrastructure, and keep participants' data with the host, shared onward only with their consent.

items.title: A path to action, and a backbone to carry it
items.summary: Draft for BLOOM to edit: people don't just want to be heard; they want what they decide together to matter. Name the decision-maker and the date before building, and decide early who keeps organizing after the last session.
items.body:
From bloom-project.org: "People don't just want to be heard. They want what they decide together to matter." BLOOM designs assemblies "around a path to action connecting what communities decide to the people and institutions that can act on it." Utah's delegates carried their recommendations to a legislative reception; Central Oregon's assembly feeds policy work in January.

In Rahmin's words: "The backbone question: who keeps organizing between and after the sessions so recommendations actually land? Worth deciding early." And across hosts: "who is helping coordinate and support that?"

Working in this frame:

- Every plan names the decision-maker (a school board, a city council, a county, a legislature), when they decide, and how the recommendations will reach them.
- Every plan names the backbone: the person or small group who keeps organizing between sessions and after the last one, and what they do the week after.
- Close the loop with participants: a results page people can return to, a printable summary, and updates on what decision-makers did with the recommendations.
- Across hosts, name who coordinates and supports the hosts themselves (BLOOM's cohort role), so no host organizes alone.

items.title: Trust starts close to home, and connects upward
items.summary: Draft for BLOOM to edit: communities take on the questions they can act on locally; questions that need more scale become the agenda for state and national assemblies. Each process leaves capacity behind.
items.body:
From bloom-project.org: "Trust starts close to home. Communities take on the questions they can act on locally; questions that require more scale become the agenda for state and national assemblies." Each local assembly connects into the Public Assembly on AI, "a growing network of in-person and online assemblies." And each one should leave behind "local organizations and residents with greater capacity to work through future public problems together."

Working in this frame:

- Name the scope a question belongs at. Build for the local decision first, and mark which findings should travel up to a state or national agenda.
- Keep "Export results" visible so a host's results can join BLOOM's reporting layer and the wider network. (The export shape is a placeholder until BLOOM shares its schema.)
- Build so the next host can run it: real local names and specifics, with a plain structure another place could lift. Say in a sentence what another host would change.
- Count capacity as an outcome: who learned to facilitate, which partners now work together, what the host can run again without outside help.

items.title: Build what people decided
items.summary: Draft for BLOOM to edit: builds help people see and test what an assembly envisions. Buildathons follow or sit inside a deliberative process, start from its recommendations, and never get ahead of what people decided.
items.body:
Rahmin's idea, being explored for Utah (attached to the assembly's published recommendations) and Central Oregon (after the December assembly): pair buildathons with deliberative processes so residents can see what they are envisioning and co-create it from shared values. Many recommendations are buildable: Utah's top proposal was a public information hub on AI decisions, alongside AI literacy through community libraries.

Working in this frame:

- Start from a recommendation, cite it, and show its level of support. The build serves what people decided; it does not stand in for deciding.
- Bring delegates and participants into the build, not just technologists. "Buildathon" lands better than "hackathon" (learned in Utah).
- Show the prototype back to the assembly, host, and decision-maker as a way to keep the recommendation moving.
- Do not build an answer to a question that is still being deliberated. Before an assembly decides, build for the process (participation, learning, sensemaking), not for an outcome.

items.title: "In partnership with BLOOM" on derived materials
items.summary: Draft for BLOOM to edit: since builds here draw on BLOOM's model, derived materials and proposals carry an "In partnership with BLOOM" credit, alongside the civic host. It matters for how the work keeps getting resourced.
items.body:
In Rahmin's words: "Attribution: since this draws on BLOOM's model, we'd want 'in partnership with BLOOM' credited on materials and in the proposal. It matters for how we keep resourcing the work."

Working in this frame:

- Apps, agendas, outreach plans, flyers, reports, and proposals that grow from this studio's shelf carry the line "In partnership with BLOOM" (footer, about page, or title block).
- Credit the civic host and its partners first and by name. BLOOM's own framing is "bigger than any one organization."
- Lineage travels with every remix: a build says what it grew from, and the studio gallery shows the chain.

items.title: Open Poll
items.summary: Draft for BLOOM to edit: BLOOM's tool for mapping the opinion landscape. People vote on short statements and add their own; voting patterns surface opinion groups and the statements every group agrees on.
items.body:
The first stage of BLOOM's stack. An Open Poll puts short statements in front of a community (agree, disagree, pass) and lets people add statements of their own. Analysis of voting patterns finds opinion groups and shows, for each statement, the percent who agree overall and by group.

In Central Oregon the Open Poll ran alongside six listening sessions and reached 400+ residents across the region. See the report: https://report.bloomproject.us/central-oregon-ai

In the Builder: a generated poll tool should produce results that can hand off to the deliberation stage and export as JSON/CSV (participants, opinion groups, statements with percent agree by group).

**What the live poll looks like** (all.bloomproject.us, Oct 2026): a location tag (USA, Utah), the question as a header ("AI and the future of our communities"), one statement at a time in quotes with a "10 left" counter, three buttons: Agree, Disagree, Unsure, a "Something wrong? Report this statement" link, and a "Share your perspective..." box at the bottom. Adding a perspective opens instructions first (share a belief, concern, or value in your own words; one idea per submission; keep it respectful; no links or URLs; a shared space with Terms of Use and a Moderation Policy; "don't overthink it, there's no wrong answer"), then a 240-character box under the poll's question. Screenshot of that flow: https://texakzqqenzpxawktbgx.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/studio-library/bloom/open-poll-perspective.png

items.title: Community conversation transcription
items.summary: Draft for BLOOM to edit: BLOOM's transcription for the live neighborhood conversations, so what people say at the tables becomes text the host can work with.
items.body:
The second stage of BLOOM's stack begins with the live conversations: listening sessions and neighborhood conversations where people work through tradeoffs in small groups. Transcription turns what is said at the tables into text, so the host can theme it, quote it, and report on it alongside the poll.

In Central Oregon, six listening sessions around the region fed quotes into the report next to the poll statements (each theme shows poll statements and session quotes side by side). See: https://report.bloomproject.us/central-oregon-ai

In the Builder: a kit should plan where and how conversations get recorded, with consent, and leave room for the transcript to flow into the themer.

items.title: Table themer
items.summary: Draft for BLOOM to edit: BLOOM's theming for table conversations. Statements and quotes from the tables get sorted into themes the host can name and work with.
items.body:
Theming is how the raw material from the tables (and the poll) becomes a shape a community can read. BLOOM's table themer sorts statements and quotes into themes; the host reads what sets each theme apart and names it.

In Central Oregon, 400+ people's responses were sorted into seven themes: Governance & Decision-Making, Data Centers, Education & Children, Mental Health, Workforce & Labor, Existential Risk, and Access to Quality Information. Each theme holds poll statements and session quotes. See: https://report.bloomproject.us/central-oregon-ai

Rahmin notes that BLOOM has also built admin interfaces for hosts to do composition, analysis, and sense-making; those are not described here.

**What the themed output looks like** in the report's Data Explorer: one colored card per theme with the theme name, "N statements · M quotes", and a row of small squares (filled for a poll statement, outlined for a session quote) that open the underlying text.

items.title: Reporting and insights layer
items.summary: Draft for BLOOM to edit: BLOOM's public report. Who participated, the opinion groups, the consensus statements with percent agree by group, the themes with statements and quotes, and a call to action.
items.body:
The last stage of BLOOM's stack: a public report that carries what a community said back to the community and to the decision-maker. The Central Oregon report walks five steps: Who participated (a map of 400+ people by town), Opinion Groups (three groups with a sentence on what distinguishes each), Consensus (statements with percent agree overall and by group), Call to Action (a Civic Assembly), and a Data Explorer (seven themes, each with poll statements and session quotes). See: https://report.bloomproject.us/central-oregon-ai

In the Builder: every generated deliberation tool exposes "Export results" as JSON/CSV in a placeholder shape (participants, opinion groups, consensus statements with percent agree by group, themes with statements and quotes) so a host's results can travel into BLOOM's report layer. The placeholder stays a placeholder until BLOOM shares the real schema.

**What the report looks like:** a hero ("What did Central Oregonians have to say about AI?", a Dive In button), then a fixed step bar (1/5 Who participated? ... 5/5 Data Explorer) with arrows. Opinion groups are stacked cards with a name, a people count pill, and one sentence on what distinguishes the group. Consensus is a card per statement: a green "Consensus (92% agree)" bar, the statement in quotes, who said it, then percent who agree by opinion group with a bar each.

items.title: Central Oregon AI: what 400+ people had to say
items.summary: Draft for BLOOM to edit: Central Oregon Civic Action Project and partners asked what should be done about AI. 400+ residents, six listening sessions plus one Open Poll, seven themes, three opinion groups, common ground on transparency and community involvement, and a Civic Assembly in December 2026.
items.body:
**Who:** Central Oregon Civic Action Project (COCAP) and its partners, with BLOOM's stack. Report: https://report.bloomproject.us/central-oregon-ai

**Question:** What did Central Oregonians have to say about AI, and what should be done about it?

**Who participated:** 400+ people across the region, through the Open Poll and six live listening sessions. The report maps participation by town: Bend (largest), Redmond, Sisters, Prineville, Madras, La Pine, and smaller places like Culver, Terrebonne, Camp Sherman, and Antelope.

**Opinion groups:** analysis of voting patterns found three.
- Optimists (51 people): see AI's arrival as inevitable, and are the least convinced it's already doing harm.
- Pragmatists (235 people): agree that AI already delivers real benefits, but want real accountability from AI companies.
- Skeptics (113 people).

**Common ground:** despite their differences, almost everyone agreed on the importance of transparency and community involvement in AI-related decision-making. The top consensus statement, 92% agree: "We need stronger transparency around how AI is being used in the education system, by teachers, administrators, and students" (a man from Sisters). By group: Optimists 96%, Pragmatists 92%, Skeptics 95%. A second consensus statement sits at 91% agree.

**Seven themes** (poll statements and session quotes in each): Governance & Decision-Making (25 statements, 4 quotes); Data Centers (12, 3); Education & Children (15, 6); Mental Health (3, 9); Workforce & Labor (19, 0); Existential Risk (10, 3); Access to Quality Information (14, 7).

**What's next:** a Civic Assembly in December 2026 where 30 to 40 residents will develop policies to make sure the public has a meaningful role in the government's AI-related decisions. Residents are invited to register; selected delegates receive a $250 stipend. The report ends with Register, Share this with a friend, and Explore the Data.

**Why it matters for hosts:** this is the whole loop in one place: map the landscape, deliberate, report, and hand the result to an assembly that carries it forward.

items.title: Neighborhood deliberation kit
items.summary: Draft for BLOOM to edit: build with this to get the whole kit for one neighborhood question: a poll-to-report app with sample data and an "Export results" placeholder for BLOOM's report layer, plus program/agenda.md, program/outreach.md, and materials/flyer.html.
items.body:
Our civic host: [the organization convening this, and the person who answers for it]
Our place: [neighborhood, school community, or town]
The question we're working through together: [one public question, in plain words]
Who needs to be heard: [parents and teachers? renters and owners? youth and elders? which languages?]
The decision-maker and their date: [who the recommendations go to, and when they decide]
The backbone: [who keeps organizing between and after the sessions]

Please produce the full kit, across this conversation:

1. **The app** (the Open Poll to report flow, demo-friendly out of the box). People pick a role, vote agree / disagree / pass on short statements one at a time, and add their own (new statements wait in a steward queue). Results open at a threshold and show opinion groups, consensus statements with percent agree overall and by group, and themes with statements and quotes. Ship a clearly labeled sample dataset (a "Sample data" switch) so a host can walk poll, opinion groups, consensus, themes, and report in two minutes without real participants; clearing it is one click. Include a visible "Export results" button that writes JSON and CSV in this placeholder shape, and say in the UI that it is a placeholder until BLOOM shares the real schema: participants (total, by place, by channel: poll or sessions), opinion_groups (id, name, size, description), consensus_statements (id, text, agree_overall_pct, agree_by_group, source), themes (name, statements, quotes with attribution).
2. **program/agenda.md**: a timeboxed facilitation agenda for a 90-minute neighborhood conversation, with the tension underneath the question and three starting prompts written in, small-group format, ground rules, and a named host.
3. **program/outreach.md**: who invites whom, where flyers go, which doors get knocked, which languages, and the weekly rhythm for the backbone.
4. **materials/flyer.html**: a printable, standalone flyer with inline styles and room for a QR code to the poll.

Credit "In partnership with BLOOM" in the app footer, the agenda, and the flyer. Say who was heard and who wasn't wherever results appear. Keep the stages visible: map the landscape first, then deliberate on tradeoffs toward supermajority agreement, then report back to the people and to the decision-maker.

**Visual references** (BLOOM's real tools, for the look and the shape of results, not to copy pixel for pixel): the poll screen https://texakzqqenzpxawktbgx.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/studio-library/bloom/open-poll.png, the add-a-perspective flow https://texakzqqenzpxawktbgx.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/studio-library/bloom/open-poll-perspective.png, opinion groups https://texakzqqenzpxawktbgx.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/studio-library/bloom/reporting-layer.png, consensus by group (attached), themes https://texakzqqenzpxawktbgx.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/studio-library/bloom/table-themer.png.

items.title: Sunset Schools Deliberation
items.summary: Draft for BLOOM to edit: a bilingual (English / Traditional Chinese) Pol.is-style poll for Francis Scott Key Elementary parents and teachers in San Francisco's Outer Sunset, on screens and AI in the classroom, ahead of SFUSD's March 2027 technology and AI policy vote. Live at https://relationalbuilder.org/s/sunset-schools-deliberation/
items.body:
**Civic host:** the Francis Scott Key Elementary parent and teacher community (Outer Sunset, San Francisco), with an editorial trio stewarding statements.

**Question:** What should technology and AI look like in our kids' classrooms at Francis Scott Key?

**Why now:** SFUSD plans to adopt a technology and AI policy in March 2027. AI is already in classrooms (a district ChatGPT Edu contract, the Amira reading tutor), and views are strong and differ: parents organizing as Tech in Check, the teachers' union UESF, SF Parents Coalition, and the district itself.

**How it works:** pick a role (parent, teacher or staff, both), vote on the deck one statement at a time in English or Traditional Chinese, add a perspective (steward-reviewed before it enters the deck). Results stay locked until 25 people have each answered 10+ statements, then show where the whole FSK community agrees, where parents and teachers agree or differ, and what divides us. People name the groups. The report is read aloud at a School Site Council meeting and becomes FSK's written input to the Board of Education.

**Live:** https://relationalbuilder.org/s/sunset-schools-deliberation/
**Code:** https://github.com/joshnesbit/sunset-delib

Remixed from the Neighborhood deliberation kit. In partnership with BLOOM.
